path.title: Testing with Playwright
path.subtitle: Tests that survive your next refactor
path.summary: Most engineering teams treat tests like a cricket umpire's signal: noisy, late, and ignored. This path teaches you the mental models behind why tests are worth the slowdown, where they belong on the pyramid, and how to write Playwright suites that catch real bugs without crying wolf at 3am. By the end you can triage a flaky e2e suite, rewrite the worst offenders, and ship a CI pipeline your on-call doesn't curse.

blocks.notesByline: Notes by Sneha, SDET batch of 2024

blocks.md:
Every engineer has a test they wish they had written. It is usually the one they didn't, the night before the bug shipped, in the code path they were sure couldn't break. Tests feel like overhead until exactly the moment they are the only thing standing between you and a 3am page from on-call.

This lesson is not a sermon. It is a defence: a clear-eyed argument for why you slow down now to go faster later, and why most teams who say *we don't have time to test* are confusing two completely different costs.

blocks.title: Mental model: tests are documentation for future-you
blocks.md:
Stop thinking of tests as a *safety net*. That metaphor makes them sound like insurance: boring, optional, paid for in case of disaster.

Think of tests as **executable documentation written in a language the runtime can verify**. Comments lie. README files go stale. The test suite is the only document that screams when reality stops matching it. The audience is not your QA team or your CI. The audience is **you, six months from now**, who has forgotten why this code exists and is one bad refactor away from breaking checkout for 12,000 paying customers.

blocks.caption: Watch a feature decay across 6 months, with and without a test suite holding it up.

hi-IN.title: Intern story #1
hi-IN.md: Scene yeh hai: intern ko bola gaya "yaar, jaldi se ek button banaa do." Intern ne button banaa diya. Test? "Bhai abhi time nahi hai, baad mein likhenge." Three months later, button bhi nahi raha, intern bhi nahi raha, lekin button ka bug *raha*. PM aaya, bola "yeh button kabse toota hai?" Kisiko nahi pata. Test hota toh git blame mein answer milta. Ab toh sirf prayer hai.
hi-IN.attribution: — heard at every Bengaluru standup, ever

en.title: Intern story #1
en.md: Classic scene: intern is told "build this button quickly." Intern builds the button. Tests? "No time, will add later." Three months on: the button is gone, the intern is gone, but the bug from the button remains. PM walks in: "how long has this been broken?" Nobody knows. A test would have left a trail in git blame. Now you have prayer.

blocks.md:
Here is the bargain a test makes with you: *I will cost you 20 minutes today, and in exchange I will catch one specific bug forever, automatically, without you having to remember it exists.*

That's it. That's the entire deal. Most engineers reject the bargain because they overestimate the 20 minutes (it's usually 5) and underestimate *forever* (it's usually a year of nightly CI runs, which is roughly 1,825 free QA passes). The math only looks bad if you assume the bug will never come back. Bugs always come back. Bugs are the cockroaches of the software world; for every one you see, twelve are hiding behind the conditional you didn't read.

**The named move:** before you write a fix, write the test that *would have caught the bug if it had existed yesterday*. The fix follows for free.

blocks.title: The regression bargain in practice

steps.label: 1. Bug arrives in prod
steps.body: On-call gets paged. Customer screenshot. Stack trace points to a `null` in checkout.

steps.label: 2. Reproduce locally
steps.body: Spend 15 min finding the input that triggers it. This is the expensive part. Don't waste it.

steps.label: 3. Write the failing test FIRST
steps.body: Before the fix. Same input. Watch it go red. This proves you actually understood the bug.

steps.label: 4. Apply the fix
steps.body: Now the fix is obvious because the test pinned down the exact behaviour you want.

steps.label: 5. Watch the test go green
steps.body: And it stays green forever. Future-you, refactoring this in 2027, gets a red CI before the bug ever ships again.

blocks.prompt: Your team finds a bug in production. What's the *first* thing you write?

choices.label: The fix, then a test once the fix is verified
choices.explain: Tempting and common, but you skip the proof that you actually understood the bug. Half the time the fix solves a *different* version of the problem and the original bug recurs in a month.

choices.label: A failing test that reproduces the bug, then the fix
choices.explain: Yes. The failing test is your evidence that you understood the bug. The fix is then mechanical and the regression is locked out forever.

choices.label: A Slack message asking who owns this code
choices.explain: Sometimes necessary, but not the *first* engineering action. Triage and reproduction come first.

choices.label: A retry with `--retries=3` to see if it goes away
choices.explain: This is how 14% flake rates are born. Retries hide bugs; they don't fix them.

hi-IN.title: QA-Aunty Anita's diagnosis
hi-IN.md: QA bola: "flaky test hai, ignore karo." Dev bola: "mere laptop pe pass hota hai." Dono right the. Dono wrong bhi the. Test flaky tha *because* dev ke laptop pe network 200ms tha aur CI pe 800ms. Real bug yeh tha ki code 500ms ke baad timeout maar raha tha. Aunty Anita ne dono ko chai pilayi aur bola "deterministic clock laga lo, drama band karo." Done.
hi-IN.attribution: — QA-Aunty Anita, after her third chai

en.title: QA-Aunty Anita's diagnosis
en.md: QA said: "it's a flaky test, ignore it." Dev said: "it passes on my laptop." Both were right. Both were wrong. The test was flaky *because* the dev's laptop had 200ms network latency and CI had 800ms. The real bug was a 500ms timeout in code. Anita made them tea and said "install a deterministic clock, stop the drama." Fixed.

blocks.md:
Now the trap. Most teams who *do* invest in tests fall for **the coverage bait**: chasing a number — 80%, 90%, the magical 100% — instead of chasing the property the test should prove. You end up with 1,400 tests, 92% line coverage, and zero confidence the checkout flow works on mobile Safari.

Coverage is a *necessary but not sufficient* signal. A test that asserts `expect(result).toBeDefined()` adds coverage and proves nothing. A test that asserts `the user can complete checkout with a 30-character UPI ID containing dots` proves something specific and valuable. The coverage tool can't tell the difference. Your code review must.

**The named move:** for every test, ask *what specific bug would this catch if it ever shipped?* If you can't answer in one sentence, the test is theatre.

coach.name: Test-Sensei Tarun
coach.role: Principal SDET, ex-Flipkart, ex-Razorpay, currently arguing with someone on r/QualityAssurance

intro: Tarun has reviewed 2,400 PRs in his career and seen every flavour of test theatre.
He'll show you 5 tests. Your job: classify each as 'real signal' (catches a bug worth catching), 'theatre' (looks like a test, isn't one), or 'just delete it' (actively harmful).

scenarios.situation: `expect(user).toBeDefined()` after calling `getUser()` that always returns a user object even on error.
scenarios.explain: This passes whether the function works or not. It's worse than no test because it gives false confidence.

scenarios.situation: `expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay ₹1,200' })).toBeVisible()` after navigating to the checkout page with a ₹1,200 cart.
scenarios.explain: Specific, role-based, asserts a behaviour a customer would notice. This is what 'real signal' looks like.

scenarios.situation: A snapshot test of the entire homepage HTML, regenerated whenever it fails.
scenarios.explain: Snapshots that get regenerated on every failure are just a slow way to ship UI changes. They prove nothing.

scenarios.situation: `expect(checkoutTotal('IN', ['UPI'])).toBe(1234)` for a function with 14 conditional branches across currency, payment method, and tax.
scenarios.explain: A specific input → specific expected output, on a function with real branching logic. This catches off-by-one and tax-rule regressions.

scenarios.situation: `expect(true).toBe(true)` left at the top of a test file 'as a placeholder' for 18 months.
scenarios.explain: Yes, this is a real PR comment from 2024. Just delete it. It pads the count and slows CI.

scenarios.situation: An e2e test that logs in, adds 3 items to cart, and asserts the cart count is `3`.
scenarios.explain: It looks like an e2e test, but the only thing it proves is that addition works. The actual checkout flow, payment, and confirmation are untested. Push the assertion further.

blocks.title: The classic trap: confusing coverage with confidence
blocks.md: A 92% coverage badge on your README does not mean your product works. It means 92% of your lines were *executed* by some test, somewhere, at some point. Whether those tests asserted anything meaningful is a different question, and the badge will not tell you. Teams that optimise for coverage end up with brittle, low-value tests; teams that optimise for *catching the bugs that would actually ship* end up with fewer tests that pull more weight.

blocks.prompt: Order these from highest-value test to lowest-value (drag to re-order, top = highest value):

items.label: Asserts the user can complete checkout end-to-end with a real payment method
items.detail: Catches the bugs that lose revenue. Slow but priceless.

items.label: Unit test for a tax calculation with 6 representative input combinations
items.detail: Fast, specific, catches the bugs that come back every quarter.

items.label: Integration test that verifies the API returns the right shape for 3 product types
items.detail: Catches contract drift between frontend and backend.

items.label: Snapshot test of a button component
items.detail: Updates whenever the button changes. Catches almost nothing.

items.label: `expect(result).toBeTruthy()` on a function that always returns an object

blocks.hint: Value comes from specificity and the cost of the bug it catches, not from how many lines it covers.

blocks.instruction: Take this real test from a Bengaluru SaaS and rewrite it so it actually proves something. The original asserts the page loaded; you want it to assert the user can do the thing the page exists for.

blocks.prompt: Which of these is a sign your test suite has fallen into the coverage bait? (Pick all that apply.)

choices.label: Coverage is 91% but a critical bug still shipped to production last week
choices.explain: Classic symptom. Coverage was high; signal was low.

choices.label: Most tests assert `toBeDefined()` or `toBeTruthy()` rather than specific behaviours
choices.explain: These assertions pass for almost any return value. They're padding, not proof.

choices.label: Your CI run takes 28 minutes because there are 1,400 tests
choices.explain: Slow CI is a separate problem. The number of tests doesn't tell you their quality on its own.

choices.label: The team panics whenever coverage drops by 0.5%
choices.explain: When the metric becomes the goal, you've lost the plot. Goodhart's Law in test form.

hi-IN.title: The 92% badge
hi-IN.md: Ek startup ne README mein '92% test coverage' ka shiny badge laga rakha tha. Investor pitch deck mein bhi tha. Three months baad, prod down. RCA mein pata chala: woh 92% mein checkout flow ka *zero* coverage tha. Bas utility functions tested the. Aunty bolti hai: "badge dikhane ke liye nahi, bug pakadne ke liye test likho."

en.title: The 92% badge
en.md: A startup had a shiny '92% test coverage' badge on their README. It was in the investor pitch deck. Three months later, prod went down. RCA revealed: that 92% had *zero* coverage of the checkout flow. Only utility functions were tested. Lesson: write tests to catch bugs, not to earn badges.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The ₹47 Lakh Refactor That Shipped on a Friday
blocks.source: Senior platform engineer at Shulka Pay, a Mumbai-based B2B payments SaaS (Series C, ~₹400 Cr ARR)
blocks.story:
Shulka's checkout service was a 9,000-line TypeScript monolith with **zero Playwright tests** and 31% statement coverage from a stale Jest suite that everyone ignored. On Friday, March 7, 2025, the platform team merged a 'low-risk' refactor: extracting the idempotency key generator into a shared package. Lint passed. Build passed. The two unit tests that touched it passed. They deployed to production at 4:42pm IST and went home.

By 7:15pm — peak settlement hour for the 200+ retailers running EOD batch payments — every third checkout was double-charging. The new idempotency generator was using `Date.now()` instead of `crypto.randomUUID()`, so two requests in the same millisecond got the same key, but **only on the new payment-link endpoint**, which the old Jest suite never covered.

Incident lasted **4 hours 18 minutes**. Total reversal volume: ₹2.3 Cr. SLA penalties to enterprise contracts: **₹47 lakh**. The post-mortem identified that a single Playwright spec — `checkout.spec.ts` clicking pay twice in 800ms — would have caught the regression in 7 seconds on the PR.

The team now has 142 Playwright specs, runs them on every PR, and has not had a checkout incident in 14 months.
blocks.takeaway: Tests don't slow you down — they slow down the bad version of the code, which is the entire point. The refactor that scares you is exactly the one your tests were written for.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The 4-Minute CTO Pitch
blocks.setup:
It's Sneha's second week as QA Lead at **Tarakash**, a Pune-based SaaS company (~150 engineers, expense-management product, ARR ₹180 Cr). She inherited a Playwright suite with a **14% flake rate**, a 38-minute CI run, and a dev team that mostly skips it with `[skip ci]`.

She walks into a Monday standup. The CTO, **Vikram**, opens with: *'I've been looking at our CI bill — ₹4.2 lakh a month, half of it on Playwright. Honestly, do we even need this suite? Our last three incidents weren't caught by tests anyway. Convince me in four minutes or I'm proposing we delete it.'*

Sneha has 240 seconds. The room is quiet.

coach.name: Staff-SDET Saurabh
coach.role: 18 years of test infra, has seen three companies delete their suites and regret it within a quarter

stages.prompt: Sneha's **opening line** sets the tone. What does she lead with?

options.label: "Tests are an industry best practice — every mature engineering org has them."
options.explain: Vikram's response: *'Best practice for whom? Show me the ROI.'* You just lost 30 seconds and the room. 'Best practice' is the weakest argument in any pitch — it's an appeal to authority a CTO will dismantle in one sentence.

options.label: "You're right that the last three incidents weren't caught — and that's exactly the problem I'm here to fix. Let me show you what they would have cost with no suite at all."
options.explain: **This is the move.** You agreed with Vikram's framing (he's not wrong — the suite *is* underperforming), then pivoted to the counterfactual: what does the world without tests look like? You bought yourself the next 3 minutes of attention.

options.label: "If we delete the suite, our SOC 2 audit fails in November."
options.explain: Compliance arguments work but they make you look like the 'no' person. Vikram will counter with 'we'll write a compensating control' and now you're in a procurement debate, not a quality conversation. Save this card for stage 3.

options.label: Open the laptop and start showing flake-rate dashboards.
options.explain: You just made the CTO's case for him — the dashboard *proves* the suite is unhealthy. Lead with the argument, then the data. Otherwise you've handed him the murder weapon.

stages.prompt: Vikram leans in. *'Okay, the counterfactual. Show me.'* What's Sneha's strongest **single example**?

options.label: The Shulka Pay ₹47 lakh checkout incident — public post-mortem, similar architecture, single missing Playwright spec.
options.explain: **Lethal.** A real, public, recent, sector-adjacent failure with a specific number. Vikram knows Shulka's CTO. The 'this could be us' lands harder than any internal data. Specificity beats abstraction every time.

options.label: A generic stat: 'Studies show e2e tests catch 23% of regressions.'
options.explain: *Which* study? On whose codebase? Vikram has read the same McKinsey deck and dismissed it. Generic stats are a tell that you don't have a real example.

options.label: Tarakash's own incident from October — the invoice-export regression that took 6 hours to detect because nobody had a smoke test on the CSV download flow.
options.explain: **Even better when paired with (a).** Internal example proves it's already happening here, external example proves the worst case. One-two punch. Vikram cannot dismiss either.

options.label: Show the test coverage report — currently at 41%.
options.explain: Coverage % is a vanity metric and Vikram knows it. He'll respond: *'We could hit 95% by testing getters. Would that prevent incidents?'* You just walked into an L5 question your stage-3 self isn't ready for.

stages.prompt: Vikram is convinced tests *can* matter. But he's still skeptical of *this* suite. *'The 14% flake rate is the real problem. Why shouldn't I just delete it and start over?'* Sneha's **counter-proposal**?

options.label: "Give me 6 weeks. I'll cut the suite to the 40 specs that cover the top-5 user journeys, drop flake under 1%, and CI under 12 minutes. If I miss, you can delete it."
options.explain: **This is leadership.** A specific bet with a deadline, a measurable success criterion, and a kill switch. Vikram now has more reason to *fund* you than to fight you. He'll say yes — CTOs love a falsifiable promise.

options.label: "Let me hire two more SDETs and rebuild from scratch."
options.explain: Two new heads × ₹35 lakh/year = ₹70 lakh ask, with no deadline and no kill switch. Vikram will say 'circle back next quarter' which is CTO for 'no.' You optimized for resources, not outcome.

options.label: "Let's just turn off retries and let the flakes fail loudly until the team fixes them."
options.explain: Within 48 hours every PR is red, the dev team riots, and Vikram's earlier proposal to delete the suite has new champions. 'Make it worse to make it better' rarely survives the first sprint.

options.label: "Keep the suite, freeze new tests, and I'll publish a weekly health report so you can monitor."
options.explain: You've committed to transparency without committing to improvement. In 4 weeks the report will say the same thing it does today, and Vikram will reopen the question with more ammunition.

stages.prompt: Vikram nods. *'Fine. Six weeks. What do you need from me right now?'* Sneha's **ask**?

options.label: "Public support. Send a Slack message after this saying you're behind the rescue plan, so PRs stop merging with `[skip ci]`."
options.explain: **Free, fast, force-multiplying.** A CTO Slack message changes the social cost of bypassing tests overnight. Costs Vikram 90 seconds, saves Sneha 3 weeks of political work.

options.label: "₹15 lakh budget for new infra and a contractor."
options.explain: You haven't shown a single result yet. Asking for budget in the same meeting where you got the 6-week bet is overplaying your hand. Earn the win first, then ask for the raise.

options.label: "Authority to block any PR that introduces a new test without a justification doc."
options.explain: Sounds disciplined, plays terribly. The dev team will revolt against the new lead's 'process tax' and your 6-week deadline becomes a death march. Save process changes for week 4.

options.label: "Let me present a 5-minute update at the next 3 standups so the team sees the trend line."
options.explain: **Solid.** Visible momentum is half the battle. If flake drops from 14% to 9% in week 2, the team starts believing — and once they believe, they'll fix flakes without being asked.

outcomes.perfect: Sneha walked out with the bet, the public endorsement, and a stand-up slot. The suite lives. **Saurabh sends her a single Slack emoji: a cricket bat.** Now go win the next 6 weeks.
outcomes.good: You saved the suite but spent political capital you'll need later. Re-read the lesson on framing — agreeing-then-pivoting is the move, not 'best practice' arguments.
outcomes.learn: The suite got deleted in the next sprint. Six months later Tarakash had three production incidents and a board-mandated quality review. Re-read the lesson — especially the section on **counterfactual ROI** and **why coverage % is a trap argument**.

points: Tests are documentation for future-you, written in a language the runtime can verify.
The regression bargain: pay 5-20 minutes today for ~1,800 free CI passes per year. The math only looks bad if you assume the bug will never come back.
When fixing a bug, write the failing test *first*. The fix becomes obvious and the bug is locked out forever.
The coverage bait is the trap of optimising for a 92% number while shipping zero real signal. Coverage is necessary, not sufficient.
For every test, ask: *what specific bug would this catch?* If you can't answer in one sentence, it's theatre.

blocks.prompt: Think about the most recent bug that shipped to production in your codebase. Could a test have caught it? Why didn't one exist? Be honest about whether the answer is 'we didn't have time' or 'we didn't have the discipline'.

blocks.md:
Most teams have an *ice-cream cone* test suite, not a pyramid: 800 e2e tests on top, 14 integration tests in the middle, 6 unit tests at the bottom (left over from when they used Jest in 2019). The CI run takes 28 minutes, the flake rate is 14%, and nobody can tell you what would actually break if a specific function changed.

The pyramid is not academic. It's a budget. Every test you add costs *something* — wall time, CI minutes, maintenance attention, on-call sleep. The shape of your suite tells you where you're spending that budget.

blocks.title: Mental model: tests live at three altitudes
blocks.md:
Think of your suite as **three altitudes of flight**:

- **Unit (ground level)** — one function, no I/O, runs in milliseconds. You write hundreds. They give you fast feedback while typing.
- **Integration (cruising altitude)** — a few units stitched together, maybe a real database, maybe a mocked API. Runs in seconds. You write dozens.
- **End-to-end (cruising stratosphere)** — the whole plane, real browser, real network, real backend. Runs in minutes. You write the *handful* that matter.

The higher you go, the slower and flakier the test. The pyramid shape isn't a style preference; it's the only shape where the suite stays runnable as you grow.

blocks.caption: Watch a feature get tested at each altitude — same logic, very different cost.

hi-IN.title: The Mumbai local analogy
hi-IN.md: Unit tests = local train. Har station rukti hai, fast hai, sasti hai, har 4 minute mein ek. Integration = express. Fewer stops, thoda mehenga, par reliable. E2E = Rajdhani. Ek hi run hota hai din mein, signal fail ho gaya toh poora schedule barbaad. Sab zaroori hai. Lekin agar tum saara traffic Rajdhani pe daal doge, station par log fight karenge.
hi-IN.attribution: — Test-Sensei Tarun, on the 7:48 Western local

en.title: The Mumbai local analogy
en.md: Unit tests are like the Mumbai local train: every stop, fast, cheap, one every 4 minutes. Integration is the express: fewer stops, slightly more expensive, reliable. E2E is the Rajdhani: one run a day, one signal failure ruins the whole schedule. All of them matter. But put all your traffic on the Rajdhani and the platform turns into a brawl.

blocks.md:
The first job of unit tests is *not coverage*. It is **fast feedback while you are still holding the problem in your head**. If a unit test takes 30 seconds to run, you'll context-switch, you'll alt-tab to Slack, and by the time the result lands you've forgotten why you cared. Unit tests should run in **single-digit milliseconds**, in the watch mode running on your second monitor, while you type.

Use them for **logic that has shape**: tax rules, currency conversion, validation, state machines. Anything where the input space is large but the function is pure. Skip them for code that is mostly *moving data from A to B* — that's what integration is for.

**The named move:** *unit-as-fast-feedback*. If your unit test makes a network call, it isn't a unit test, it's a slow integration test in a costume. Mock the I/O or move the test up the pyramid.

blocks.title: Translation: turning a bug report into the right test, at the right altitude

steps.label: 1. The customer report
steps.body: "When I check out with a UPI ID that has a dot, like sneha.s@okhdfc, the total shows ₹0."

steps.label: 2. Where does the logic live?
steps.body: The bug is in the `formatUpiId()` function. Pure input → output. No network, no DOM. This screams unit test.

steps.label: 3. Write the unit test
steps.body: Three lines. Runs in 4ms. No browser, no DB.

steps.label: 4. Resist the urge to write an e2e
steps.body: An e2e test for this would take 90 seconds, hit a real Razorpay sandbox, and prove the same thing as the 4ms unit test.

steps.label: 5. Add ONE e2e for the critical path
steps.body: Yes — *one* test that proves checkout end-to-end works for a UPI user. The unit test catches the formatting bug; the e2e catches the wiring.

blocks.prompt: Which of these is *not* appropriate for a unit test?

choices.label: A function that calculates GST on a cart total based on item categories
choices.explain: Pure logic with branching. Perfect unit test territory.

choices.label: A reducer in a state machine that transitions cart states
choices.explain: Pure function, deterministic, fast. Ideal for a unit test.

choices.label: A test that fills a form, clicks Submit, and asserts the user is redirected to a confirmation page
choices.explain: This is an e2e test pretending to be a unit test. The DOM, the router, and the backend are all involved. Move it up the pyramid.

choices.label: A function that validates an Indian phone number format
choices.explain: Pure regex/validation logic. Classic unit test.

hi-IN.title: The Selenium widow
hi-IN.md: Pune ki ek QA team thi, 2,200 Selenium tests. Run karne mein 4 ghante. Maintenance lead bhaag gaya, 'I'm done.' Naye lead ne chart banaya: 2,200 mein se 86 tests asli bug pakadte the. Baaki 2,114 sirf CI ka bijli bill badha rahe the. Unit + integration + 86 e2e mein migrate kiya. Ab run 11 minute. Lead ki neend wapas aa gayi.
hi-IN.attribution: — a true story, names changed to protect the formerly sleep-deprived

en.title: The Selenium widow
en.md: A Pune QA team had 2,200 Selenium tests. The full run took 4 hours. The maintenance lead quit: 'I'm done.' The new lead drew a chart: of the 2,200 tests, 86 had ever caught a real bug. The other 2,114 just inflated the CI electricity bill. They migrated to unit + integration + 86 e2e tests. Run time: 11 minutes. The lead now sleeps.

blocks.text: Move 2 — E2E for the critical path

blocks.md:
Now the top of the pyramid. **End-to-end tests are not for everything**. They are for the *critical path*: the small set of user journeys where a regression would cost you actual money or actual customers. For most products, that list is shorter than you think — 5 to 15 flows, not 500.

For a B2B SaaS like our Pune team: signup, login, the primary feature, billing, and a couple of admin flows. Total: 11 e2e tests. Each test is *important*, *visible*, and *worth the 30-second runtime*. Everything else either belongs in integration (does the API contract hold?) or unit (does this function still produce the right output?).

**The named move:** *e2e for the critical path*. Before adding an e2e test, ask: "if this test is broken on Friday and I push the broken version to prod, who calls me first — the CEO, the customer, or nobody?" If the answer is *nobody*, push the test down the pyramid.

coach.role: Principal SDET, today wearing a t-shirt that says 'flake ≠ feature'

intro: You're triaging a backlog of test ideas from your PM. Tarun is sitting next to you.
Classify each by altitude: unit, integration, or e2e (or 'don't write a test for this').

scenarios.situation: A function that converts amounts to Indian numbering format (1,00,000 instead of 100,000).
scenarios.explain: Pure transformation, no I/O. A unit test runs in 1ms and covers 8 edge cases at once.

scenarios.situation: Verifying that the `/api/invoices` endpoint returns the right JSON shape when a user has 0, 1, and 50 invoices.
scenarios.explain: Hits a real handler and a real (or test) database. Faster than e2e, more realistic than unit.

scenarios.situation: Verifying that a logged-in user can view, download, and email an invoice from the dashboard.
scenarios.explain: Critical path: full browser, full backend, end-user journey. Worth the 25 seconds.

scenarios.situation: Verifying that the 'Forgot password' page has the correct H1 text 'Reset your password'.
scenarios.explain: If you must test this, snapshot a render in jsdom. An e2e for copy is overkill; an integration is wasteful.

scenarios.situation: Verifying that the Razorpay webhook handler updates the subscription status when payment succeeds.
scenarios.explain: Backend-only flow, mock the webhook payload, hit your handler, assert DB state. Don't drive a browser for a server-side flow.

scenarios.situation: Verifying the new sidebar tooltip says 'Beta'.
scenarios.explain: If at all. Component-level unit. Burning an e2e on tooltip text is a flake-factory.

blocks.caption: Watch the trap happen live — and the fix at the end.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the inverted pyramid (the ice-cream cone)
blocks.md:
Teams build the cone for one of two reasons: either they hired a contractor who wrote 800 Selenium tests in 2019 and called it a day, or they confused *e2e* with *real testing* and treated unit tests as second-class citizens. Both end in the same place: 28-minute CI runs, 14% flake rates, and devs who learn to ignore the suite.

The fix is not to delete the e2e tests — it's to *rewrite the same coverage at a lower altitude*. For every e2e test you can demote to integration, you save ~25 seconds per CI run and remove ~3% of your flake surface.

blocks.prompt: You inherited a codebase with 800 e2e tests. Order these triage steps from first to last:

items.label: Run the suite once with `--reporter=json` and dump the per-test duration + pass rate
Sort by `(duration × flake_rate)` — these are the most expensive tests
For each top-20 test, identify the *thing being verified* in one sentence
Decide which can be rewritten at a lower altitude (unit or integration)
Rewrite 3-5 per week; keep the e2e until the lower-altitude version proves it
Delete the redundant e2e once the lower test has been green for 30 days

blocks.hint: Measure first, then choose what to demote, then rewrite, then delete. Order matters; deleting before measuring is how you lose coverage.

blocks.instruction: Here's an e2e test that's overkill for what it actually proves. Rewrite it as the right altitude (likely integration or unit). Use real Playwright APIs.

blocks.prompt: Which signs suggest your suite is shaped like an ice-cream cone, not a pyramid? (Pick all that apply.)

choices.label: CI takes 28 minutes and most of it is a single e2e shard
choices.explain: Heavy e2e weight = top-heavy suite. Classic cone.

choices.label: Devs run unit tests locally but skip e2e until CI tells them what's broken
choices.explain: This is normal. The pyramid expects fast tests local, slow tests in CI.

choices.label: You have more snapshot tests than logic tests for a pure data-transformation library
choices.explain: Snapshots over assertions is a different bait, but symptomatic of the same 'shape over substance' culture.

choices.label: When a unit test fails, you debug for an hour because three other unit tests also failed downstream
choices.explain: That's a coupling problem in your code, not a pyramid problem.

hi-IN.title: The 4am page
hi-IN.md: On-call ko 4am page aaya: e2e suite red. Half-asleep dev ne dekha — ek tooltip text change hua tha 'New' se 'New!'. 47 e2e tests assert kar rahe the exact text. Dev ne sab fix kiya, push kiya, wapas soya. 6am page aaya: ab dusri tooltip ka text change hua tha. Yeh pyramid ka inverse hai. Tooltip text ke liye e2e nahi likhte, bhai.

en.title: The 4am page
en.md: On-call gets paged at 4am: e2e suite is red. Half-asleep dev investigates: a tooltip text changed from 'New' to 'New!'. 47 e2e tests asserted the exact string. They fixed all 47, pushed, went back to sleep. 6am: page again. Different tooltip. This is the inverse pyramid. You don't write e2e tests for tooltip copy.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The 4-Hour CI That Became a 22-Minute CI
blocks.source: Engineering manager at Vyaapar Cloud, a Hyderabad-based GST-filing SaaS (~80 engineers, 1.4 lakh SMB customers)
blocks.story:
When the new EM joined Vyaapar in October 2024, the test suite looked like a team that had read 'always test the user flow' as an instruction, not a heuristic. The breakdown:

- **3 unit tests.** Two of them tested `Math.floor`. One tested a constant.
- **9 integration tests.** All flaky.
- **214 Playwright e2e specs.** Average duration 7.2s. Total CI runtime: **4 hours 11 minutes** on a 4-shard runner. Flake rate: 19%.

Devs had stopped reading test failures by August. A merge-to-main average of 3 days had become 8.

The rebuild took 6 weeks. The new pyramid:

- **840 unit tests** (Vitest, ~14s total) — every pure function, every reducer, every formatter
- **62 integration tests** (Vitest + msw, ~90s) — every server action, every API route
- **38 Playwright e2e specs** (~6 min sharded × 4) — only the top 8 user journeys, plus the 4 paths that had caused production incidents

Total CI runtime: **22 minutes**. Flake rate: 0.6%. Bugs caught at PR-time **doubled**, because faster feedback meant devs actually waited for green before merging. Merge-to-main is now 11 hours, p50.

The deleted 176 e2e specs were not 'lost coverage.' They were duplicate coverage at 50× the cost. Most had been testing the same login flow with cosmetic variations.
blocks.takeaway: The pyramid isn't dogma — it's economics. Each altitude costs ~10× the one below it. Inverted pyramids don't fall over because the geometry is wrong; they fall over because the bill comes due.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Auditing Tarakash's Test Mix
blocks.setup:
Week 2 of Sneha's 6-week rescue. She's done a triage of the existing suite at **Tarakash**:

- 47 unit tests (most testing trivial getters)
- 12 integration tests (8 of which are commented out)
- **289 Playwright e2e specs**, of which:
  - 71 test the login flow with minor variations
  - 44 test the same 'create expense' happy path
  - 31 are skipped with `test.skip(...)` and a TODO from 2024
  - The remaining 143 cover ~5 actual user journeys, with heavy redundancy

CI takes 38 minutes. Flake rate is 14%. Sneha has to write a one-page memo to the platform team recommending **what to cut, what to add, and at which altitude**.

coach.name: Staff-SDET Saurabh
coach.role: Treats the test pyramid like the Bhagavad Gita — quotes it without warning

stages.prompt: First call: the **71 login specs**. What does Sneha recommend?

options.label: Delete 68 of them. Keep 1 e2e (happy path login → dashboard). Move the rest to unit tests on the auth reducer + 2 integration tests on the `/api/auth/login` route.
options.explain: **Correct.** Login is one user journey, not 71. The variations (wrong password, locked account, MFA prompt, etc.) belong in unit tests on the auth state machine. You'll go from ~6 min of CI to ~8 seconds for the same coverage.

options.label: Keep all 71 — login is critical, more tests = more safety.
options.explain: Saurabh sighs. Login *is* critical, which is why you want it tested *fast and reliably*, not 71 times slowly. More e2e ≠ more safety; it means more flake, slower CI, and devs ignoring failures.

options.label: Keep all 71 but parallelize them across more shards.
options.explain: You're paying ~₹40k/month more in CI compute to run a suite that's still 71× redundant. Sharding hides the smell, doesn't fix the rot.

options.label: Delete all 71. Trust manual QA on login.
options.explain: Manual QA on every PR doesn't scale and won't happen. You correctly identified the redundancy but threw out the safety net with the bathwater. The lesson is to *re-platform* the coverage, not abandon it.

stages.prompt: Next: the **31 skipped specs** with TODOs from 2024. What's the move?

options.label: Delete all 31. Open one ticket for 'evaluate skipped test scenarios' if the team wants to revisit later.
options.explain: **Yes.** A skipped test is a lie — it looks like coverage, provides none, and rots in the repo. Delete them. The git history exists if you need them back, and the 'maybe later' ticket gives the team an out without keeping dead code in the suite.

options.label: Un-skip them all and fix whatever's broken.
options.explain: You just added 31 likely-broken specs to a suite already at 14% flake. Devs revolt by Friday. Fixing 18-month-old skipped tests is rarely worth it — the code under test has changed, the assumptions are stale.

options.label: Leave them skipped — they're not hurting anyone.
options.explain: They are. They confuse new joiners ('why is this skipped?'), they show up in coverage reports, and they signal 'we don't take this suite seriously' to everyone who reads the repo. Dead code is debt.

options.label: Convert them to a TODO list in `docs/test-backlog.md` and delete the spec files.
options.explain: **Even cleaner.** Captures the intent (so it's not lost) without the cost. The doc is the right place for 'here are scenarios we considered'; the spec file is not.

stages.prompt: Now the additions. Tarakash has **zero integration tests** for its 64 server actions. Sneha's recommendation?

options.label: Add ~50 integration tests using Vitest + a test database, covering every server action that touches money or auth. Skip getters and pure read paths — those go in unit tests.
options.explain: **This is the missing middle.** Integration tests for server actions catch the bugs that unit tests can't see (DB constraints, transaction boundaries) and that e2e shouldn't have to (you don't need to drive a browser to know the action returns a 422 on bad input).

options.label: Skip integration tests; cover the actions with Playwright e2e specs.
options.explain: You'd be adding 50 e2e specs at ~8s each = ~7 minutes more CI, with higher flake, to test logic a 200ms integration test would cover. This is exactly the inverted-pyramid mistake the field notes describe.

options.label: Cover them with unit tests and mock the database.
options.explain: Unit tests with mocked DBs prove your code matches your mocks, not that it matches reality. Server actions live and die at the DB boundary — that's what you have to test.

options.label: Add ~50 integration tests, but only for the 12 actions with the most production incidents in the last 6 months.
options.explain: **Pragmatic.** Coverage targeted by incident history is the highest-ROI you can buy. The other 38 can come later — start where you've already paid in pain.

outcomes.perfect: The memo lands. Platform agrees to cut 220 e2e specs, add 50 integration tests, and re-platform login coverage. Saurabh DMs you: *'You just bought back 16 minutes of CI per PR. Multiply by 80 devs × 4 PRs/day. That's ₹38 lakh of dev time per quarter.'*
outcomes.good: Reasonable cuts but you left some redundancy and skipped the integration-test add. Re-read the section on **the missing middle** — integration tests are usually the highest-ROI tier nobody writes.
outcomes.learn: You either cut too aggressively (no safety net) or too timidly (CI still 30+ min). Re-read the lesson — especially **why the pyramid is economics, not dogma** and **how to decide which e2e specs earn their seat**.

points: Tests live at three altitudes — unit, integration, e2e — each with a different cost-to-confidence ratio.
Unit-as-fast-feedback: if your unit test makes a network call, it isn't a unit test. It's a slow integration test in costume.
E2E for the critical path: the question is *who calls if this breaks?* If the answer is 'nobody', push the test down.
The ice-cream cone (lots of e2e, few unit) is the most common shape and the most expensive one. The fix is to rewrite, not delete.
Measure (duration × flake rate) before triaging. Deleting tests blind is how teams lose real coverage.

blocks.prompt: What's the *shape* of your test suite right now? If you had to draw it on a whiteboard, would it be a pyramid, an ice-cream cone, or a triangle missing its base? What's the cheapest single change you could make this week to shift the shape?

blocks.notesByline: Notes by Sneha, SDET batch of 2024

blocks.md:
Selenium veterans show up to Playwright and immediately write the same test they wrote in 2018: `await driver.findElement(By.css('.btn.btn-primary.checkout-btn-v2'))` followed by `await driver.sleep(3000)` followed by an assertion that lies because the page hadn't finished hydrating. Playwright doesn't need any of that, but the muscle memory is hard to break.

This lesson is about the two things Playwright does differently and the two named moves that make your tests resilient. By the end you'll write tests that survive a designer renaming half your CSS classes.

blocks.title: Mental model: Playwright auto-waits, stop sleeping
blocks.md:
Every Playwright action — `click`, `fill`, `selectOption`, `expect(...).toBeVisible()` — does **actionability checks** before it runs. It waits for the element to be attached, visible, stable, enabled, and on top. It retries assertions until they pass or the timeout (default 5 seconds) hits.

This means: **you almost never need `waitForTimeout`**. If your test sleeps, your test is wrong. The only legitimate uses for arbitrary sleep are (1) you genuinely cannot detect when a long-running animation has stopped, and (2) you're debugging. Both should be temporary. Anything else is a flake-factory you'll regret in 3 months.

blocks.md:
**CSS selectors are the problem, not the solution.** When you write `page.locator('.btn.btn-primary.checkout-v2')`, you're coupling your test to your designer's mood. Half your test failures will come from style refactors that did not change a single user-visible thing.

Playwright's role-based locators are the opposite: they identify elements the way a screen reader (and a human) does. `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay ₹1,200' })` finds the button labelled "Pay ₹1,200" regardless of class names, regardless of whether it's a `<button>` or a `<div role='button'>`, regardless of which framework re-rendered it last.

The locator priority you should burn into your fingertips:

1. `getByRole` — for anything interactive. The default.
2. `getByLabel` — for form fields with visible labels.
3. `getByText` — for static content you're verifying.
4. `getByTestId` — for elements with no useful semantics, where the team agrees on a `data-testid`.
5. CSS / XPath — only when the above genuinely don't work. With a comment explaining why.

**The named move:** *getByRole over CSS*. If you're reaching for `.locator('.foo')` your first instinct should be: "is there a role here I'm ignoring?"

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Rewriting the Most Important Test at Tarakash
blocks.setup:
Week 3. Sneha is rewriting Tarakash's most critical Playwright spec: the **'submit-and-approve expense'** flow. It's the path that touches money, runs on every PR, and currently fails ~9% of the time with cryptic errors.

The current spec is 84 lines of CSS selectors, hardcoded waits, and one `page.waitForTimeout(3000)` that someone added in 2023 with the comment `// flaky, fix later`.

Sneha is going to rewrite it stage-by-stage in front of two junior QA engineers. Each decision is a teaching moment.

coach.name: QA-Director Kavya
coach.role: Has personally deleted more `waitForTimeout` calls than she can count

stages.prompt: First action: clicking the **'New Expense' button** in the top nav. The current code is `await page.click('header > div.nav > button.btn-primary:nth-child(3)')`. Sneha rewrites it as?

options.label: `await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'New expense' }).click();`
options.explain: **Clean.** Role + accessible name. Survives any CSS refactor, any nav reorder, any framework migration. It also doubles as an accessibility check — if the button has no accessible name, this fails *for the right reason*.

options.label: `await page.click('[data-testid="new-expense-btn"]');` after adding the testid to the component.
options.explain: **Acceptable, with caveats.** `data-testid` is durable but it's a footnote selector — it tests an annotation, not a behavior. Use it only when the role-based locator genuinely doesn't disambiguate. Here, the role-based one is better.

options.label: `await page.click('button:has-text("New expense")');`
options.explain: Half-right. It's better than the CSS chain, but if there are multiple 'New expense' buttons on the page (e.g. in a modal that opens later) you'll get strict-mode violations or wrong clicks. `getByRole` with a name is more precise.

options.label: Keep the original — if it's working today, why change it?
options.explain: It *isn't* working today — the spec is in the 9% flake bucket, and `nth-child(3)` is a time bomb that detonates the next time someone reorders the nav. The whole point of the rescue is to stop shipping fragility.

stages.prompt: After clicking, a modal slides in. Current code: `await page.waitForTimeout(800);` then fills the form. What does Sneha replace it with?

options.label: `await expect(page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'New expense' })).toBeVisible();` then proceed.
options.explain: **This is the way.** Web-first assertions wait *for the actual condition* up to the configured timeout (5s default). No magic numbers. If the modal opens in 80ms, you wait 80ms. If it's slow that day, you wait however long it takes. No more flake from animation timing.

options.label: `await page.waitForTimeout(2000);` to be safe.
options.explain: Kavya's eye twitches. Doubling the sleep doesn't fix flake — it just hides it longer. If your test sleeps, your test is wrong. Every `waitForTimeout` is either too short (still flaky) or too long (slow CI).

options.label: `await page.locator('.modal').waitFor({ state: 'visible' });`
options.explain: Closer, but you've gone back to a CSS selector for the modal *and* you're using the older `waitFor` API. Web-first `expect(...).toBeVisible()` retries the assertion automatically and produces a much better error message on failure.

options.label: `await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');`
options.explain: `networkidle` is the wrong tool — it waits for *all* network activity to stop, which a modern app with polling/analytics never does. The Playwright docs explicitly warn against this for SPAs. You'll either wait 30s or time out.

stages.prompt: Form is filled. Sneha clicks **Submit** and needs to verify a success toast appears, then disappears. Current code waits 3 seconds then asserts. New version?

options.label: `await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Expense submitted');` then `await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toBeHidden();`
options.explain: **Two assertions, both retrying, no sleeps.** First waits up to 5s for the toast to *appear* with the right text; second waits up to 5s for it to *disappear*. Reads exactly like the user's experience and fails with crisp error messages.

options.label: `await page.waitForSelector('.toast-success'); await page.waitForTimeout(3000); await expect(page.locator('.toast-success')).toBeHidden();`
options.explain: You snuck a `waitForTimeout` back in. If the toast disappears in 2s on a fast CI runner, you wasted 1s. If it takes 3.5s on a slow one, you fail. Web-first assertions handle both.

options.label: Just check the URL changed: `await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/expenses\/[0-9]+$/);`
options.explain: **Different angle, also good.** A successful submit redirects to the new expense page — asserting the URL pattern is a strong, fast, behavior-based signal. Best paired with the toast assertion, but valid on its own.

options.label: `await page.evaluate(() => document.querySelector('.toast-success').textContent);` and string-match the result.
options.explain: You bypassed Playwright's auto-wait, dropped into raw DOM, and set yourself up for a `null` reference if the toast hasn't rendered yet. This is the kind of code that adds two more `waitForTimeout` calls within a sprint.

stages.prompt: Last decision. The spec needs to verify the expense appears in the list, but the list is paginated and the new expense is on **page 2**. What does Sneha do?

options.label: Navigate to the list, click 'Next page', then `await expect(page.getByRole('row', { name: /Lunch with client.*₹2,400/ })).toBeVisible();`
options.explain: Brittle: depends on pagination order which may change with sort options. Also makes the test slower. There's a better signal available — keep going.

options.label: Filter the list by the expense title using the search box, then assert the row is visible.
options.explain: **Realistic and resilient.** This is what a user does to find a specific item. The search filter is a stable interaction and doesn't depend on pagination order or default sort.

options.label: Hit the API directly: `const res = await request.get('/api/expenses?title=Lunch'); expect(res.json().data).toHaveLength(1);`
options.explain: **Best of both worlds.** Playwright's API request fixture lets you verify the data without driving the UI through pagination. Fast, deterministic, and tests the right boundary. Pair with one UI assertion that the new expense is *findable* in the UI.

options.label: Skip the verification — if Submit returned 200, it's in the list.
options.explain: Assuming the API call succeeded means the row is in the UI is exactly the kind of leap that produces 'it worked in CI but not in prod' bugs. The whole point of e2e is to verify the UI shows what the API saved.

outcomes.perfect: The rewritten spec is 31 lines, runs in 4.2 seconds, and has not flaked in 200 consecutive runs. Kavya tells the juniors: *'This is what a Playwright test should read like — a sentence about user behavior, not a sentence about the DOM.'*
outcomes.good: You replaced most of the CSS selectors and killed most of the sleeps, but one `waitForTimeout` slipped through or you reached for `data-testid` when `getByRole` would have worked. Re-read the lesson on **locator priority** — role first, label second, testid only as a last resort.
outcomes.learn: The rewrite still uses CSS chains or hardcoded waits. The spec will break on the next Tailwind upgrade and flake on the next slow CI runner. Re-read the lesson — especially **why web-first assertions exist** and **the locator priority order**.

points: Playwright auto-waits for elements to be actionable. If your test sleeps, your test is wrong.
Reach for getByRole first. CSS selectors are the problem, not the solution.
Web-first assertions (`expect(locator).to...()`) auto-retry. If you extract the value to a variable first, you've broken the retry loop.
The locator priority ladder: role → label → text → test ID → CSS, in that order. The bottom rungs should sting to use.
Tests that read like the user journey survive design refactors. Tests coupled to class names die in them.

blocks.prompt: Open one of your existing Playwright (or Selenium / Cypress) tests right now. How many CSS selectors does it use? How many sleeps? How many assertions extract a value before checking it? Pick one of those three and rewrite a single test to remove them. Notice how much shorter the file gets.

blocks.md:
There's an on-call engineer at a Bengaluru fintech who got paged at 3am because a Playwright test `await page.waitForTimeout(3000)`'d on a flow that, on AWS that night, took 3,200 milliseconds. The test went red. CI auto-rolled back a green deploy. Customers couldn't transact for 47 minutes. The post-mortem blamed "test flakiness."

The post-mortem was wrong. The flake was a *symptom*. The actual bug was that the team had been treating flake as noise instead of as data.

This lesson teaches you to read flake the way a doctor reads a fever: not as a thing to suppress, but as a signal pointing at the actual problem.

blocks.title: Mental model: flake is information you haven't decoded yet
blocks.md:
Most teams treat a flaky test as a bug *in the test*. Sometimes it is. More often, it's a bug in your **timing assumptions**: you assumed a network call always takes <500ms, the page always finishes hydrating in <200ms, the spinner always appears before the real content. The test passes 95% of the time because those assumptions hold 95% of the time. The other 5% is reality.

The shift in mindset: **a flaky test has discovered a non-determinism in your system you didn't know existed.** The test isn't lying. It's whistleblowing. Your job is to decode the message and either (a) fix the actual non-determinism or (b) tell the test about the timing reality so it can wait correctly.

hi-IN.title: On-call ko 3am page

blocks.prompt: A test fails 3% of the time in CI. What's your *first* move?

choices.label: Add `await page.waitForTimeout(2000)` before the failing assertion
choices.explain: This buries the signal under a sleep. The next time the underlying issue takes 2.1 seconds, you're back to flaky. Worse: you've taught the team that sleep is a fix.

choices.label: Open the trace viewer for the failing run and read the timeline + network panel
choices.explain: Right. The trace will tell you in 60 seconds whether the test is wrong, the app is wrong, or your timing assumption is wrong.

choices.label: Bump `--retries` from 2 to 5 and ship the PR
choices.explain: Retries hide flake; they don't fix it. They also slow CI by 2.5x for the failing tests. Do not pass go.

choices.label: Mark the test as `test.skip()` with a `// TODO: fix later` comment
choices.explain: The test had information for you. Now it has been gagged. The bug it was catching will eventually ship to prod.

coach.name: Test-Sensei Tarun
coach.role: Principal SDET, today wearing a hoodie that reads '`waitForTimeout` is a code smell'

intro: You're on the rotation triaging 6 flaky test reports from the team's #qa-help Slack channel.
For each, classify the *root cause*: is this a clock/timing issue, a network issue, a bad locator, or a real product bug?

scenarios.situation: Test fails ~3% of runs on the search page. Trace shows the search results appear at 290ms one time, 310ms the next. Test asserts visible at 300ms.
scenarios.explain: Classic debounce race. Install `page.clock` and advance time deterministically.

scenarios.situation: Test for the dashboard fails when the staging API returns 502 Bad Gateway during the morning deploy window.
scenarios.explain: Mock the API with `page.route()` for the test. Don't depend on a real backend's mood.

scenarios.situation: Test passes alone, fails when run in parallel with other tests. Trace shows the locator `getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })` matched 3 buttons.
scenarios.explain: Two open dialogs in the test environment have a 'Save' button. Scope the locator to the dialog: `page.getByRole('dialog').getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })`.

scenarios.situation: Test fails when the user has more than 50 invoices. The pagination logic skips the last page.
scenarios.explain: Real off-by-one. The test caught a product bug. Fix the code, not the test.

scenarios.situation: Test for the Razorpay webhook flow fails because the test database hasn't seeded the new schema field.
scenarios.explain: More precisely: a test-fixture / setup issue. Mock the webhook payload or fix the seed. Don't add a sleep hoping it'll appear.

scenarios.situation: Test for the announcement banner fails on the second run because the modal-dismissed cookie persists across tests.
scenarios.explain: Loosely: state leakage. Use a fresh browser context per test (Playwright does this by default; somebody disabled it). Locator was fine, isolation wasn't.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the retry crutch
blocks.md:
Setting `retries: 3` in `playwright.config.ts` and calling it a fix is the developer equivalent of pressing snooze. Each retry hides a real signal: the test failed, you didn't read the trace, you re-ran until it passed, and you shipped.

Retries have one legitimate use: **smoothing over genuinely random infrastructure noise** (a flaky CI runner, a transient DNS hiccup) so your CI dashboard isn't a wall of red. They are *not* a substitute for the trace-viewer ritual or the deterministic-clock fix. A team that trends `retry rate` per week and does not let it grow has a healthy suite. A team that sets `retries: 5` and looks the other way is two months from disaster.

blocks.prompt: A test starts flaking this morning. Order your debugging steps:

items.label: Reproduce locally with `--repeat-each=20` to confirm the flake exists
Open the trace viewer for the most recent failing CI run
Look at the failing step's screenshot, locator, and network panel
Form a single hypothesis (race condition? locator? real bug?)
Apply the targeted fix (clock, mock, scoped locator, or product fix)
Run `--repeat-each=50` to verify the fix and update the failure-budget log

blocks.hint: Reproduce → trace → hypothesise → fix → verify. If you skip step 2, you'll spend 4 hours guessing.

blocks.instruction: This test is flaky. Rewrite it using `page.clock` and `page.route()` so it's deterministic. The test verifies that a debounced search shows results from the API after the user stops typing for 300ms.

blocks.prompt: Which of these are *legitimate* reasons to use `--retries` in CI? (Pick all that apply.)

choices.label: Smoothing over a known-flaky CI runner so dashboards aren't all red while you fix it
choices.explain: Acceptable as a temporary measure with a tracked deadline. Not a permanent solution.

choices.label: Hiding a debounce race so you can ship the PR before the demo
choices.explain: This is exactly the trap. Use `page.clock` and ship a real fix. Demos don't excuse buried signals.

choices.label: As a final guard against transient network blips between CI and a third-party service
choices.explain: Acceptable when the third party is genuinely flaky and outside your control. Better: mock the third party with `page.route()` if possible.

choices.label: Because the team agreed flakes are 'normal' and 3 retries usually works
choices.explain: Cultural version of the trap. The day a real bug starts flaking 51% of the time, your retry strategy ships it to prod.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 14 Days of Flake, One Race Condition, Forty-Seven Engineering Hours
blocks.source: Platform engineer at Anant Labs, a Gurugram-based data-platform startup (Series B, ~110 engineers)
blocks.story:
Anant's onboarding suite started flaking on April 2, 2025. By April 16 — fourteen calendar days later — the team had logged **47 engineering hours** across six engineers triaging the same handful of specs. Every theory died:

- 'It's the CI runner's CPU.' Not it — flaked on dedicated machines too.
- 'It's network calls.' Not it — fully mocked.
- 'It's a Playwright bug.' Not it — pinned to v1.42 throughout.
- 'Just add retries.' Made it worse — masked the signal.

The breakthrough came from one trace file. An SDET opened the trace viewer (`npx playwright show-trace trace.zip`), scrubbed to the failing assertion, and saw it: the spec called `await page.click('Save')` immediately after a state update, and the save button's `onClick` handler was racing with React's re-render. The previous click handler was still attached when Playwright clicked, so the click was registered against the *old* component, which silently no-op'd.

The original 'fix' someone had added was `await page.waitForTimeout(2000)` — which masked the race ~92% of the time. That's why the flake rate looked like 8%, not 80%.

The real fix was three lines: replace the timeout with `await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })).toBeEnabled();` so Playwright waits for the button to actually be ready. Flake rate dropped from **8% to 0.4%** overnight. The trace viewer found in 20 minutes what 47 hours of guessing couldn't.
blocks.takeaway: Flake is never random — it's a race condition you haven't read carefully enough. Open the trace before you open Stack Overflow.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Three Flaky Tests, Three Trace Files
blocks.setup:
Week 4. Sneha has dropped Tarakash's overall flake rate from 14% to 4.1% by deleting the worst-offending specs. She's now down to **three persistent flakes** that resist every easy fix. CI has a 22% chance of going red on any given PR, and the dev team is starting to ignore failures again.

For each flaky spec, Sneha has a Playwright trace file from the most recent failure. She has 90 minutes before the engineering all-hands where she has to report progress. **Three diagnoses, three fixes, no guessing.**

coach.name: QA-Director Kavya
coach.role: Believes the trace viewer is the single most under-used tool in software engineering

stages.prompt: **Flaky test #1: `dashboard-greeting.spec.ts`** — fails ~6% of the time on `expect(page.getByText('Good morning')).toBeVisible()`. The trace shows the assertion failed at 11:59:58.421 IST. What does Sneha conclude?

options.label: It's a time-of-day bug — the test asserts 'Good morning' but ran at 11:59pm. Fix: mock the system clock with `await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-01-15T09:00:00') });`
options.explain: **Lethal diagnosis.** The trace timestamp is the smoking gun — at 11:59pm IST the dashboard rightfully showed 'Good evening' or 'Good night.' Playwright's clock fixture (added in v1.45) lets you freeze time per-test. No more time-of-day flake.

options.label: Add a retry: `test.describe.configure({ retries: 3 });` so the test passes on the second attempt.
options.explain: Kavya groans. The test would still fail at 11:59pm — it would just fail three times in a row. Retries are for genuinely transient failures (network blips), not for design defects you haven't bothered to find.

options.label: Loosen the assertion to `expect(page.getByText(/Good (morning|afternoon|evening|night)/)).toBeVisible();`
options.explain: You made the test never fail, which is not the same as making the test correct. Now if the greeting component breaks entirely and shows nothing, your test still passes. Looser assertions = lower signal.

options.label: Skip the test in CI between 11pm and 6am IST.
options.explain: Adding time-of-day skip logic is a complexity tax that someone else will trip over. Mocking the clock is one line; conditional skipping is a maintenance burden forever.

stages.prompt: **Flaky test #2: `expense-list.spec.ts`** — fails ~4% of the time on `await expect(rows).toHaveCount(20)`. Trace shows the page loaded with 19 rows visible, then the assertion failed, then a 20th row appeared 600ms later. Diagnosis?

options.label: It's an infinite-scroll / lazy-load race. The list paginates as you scroll; the test asserted before the last row had been requested. Fix: scroll to the bottom and wait for the loading spinner to disappear before asserting.
options.explain: **Correct read of the trace.** The 600ms gap and the appearing row are the tell. The fix: `await page.getByRole('main').evaluate(el => el.scrollTo(0, el.scrollHeight)); await expect(page.getByRole('progressbar')).toBeHidden(); await expect(rows).toHaveCount(20);`

options.label: It's a backend pagination bug. Open a ticket for the platform team.
options.explain: The trace clearly shows the row *did* appear, just late. The product is working as designed (lazy loading). The test is wrong, not the backend. You'd burn a week of platform team time finding nothing.

options.label: Add `await page.waitForTimeout(1000);` before the assertion.
options.explain: If your test sleeps, your test is wrong. The 1000ms might cover the 600ms today, but the day a slow CI runner makes it 1100ms, you're back to flake.

options.label: Change the assertion to `await expect(rows).toHaveCount(20, { timeout: 5000 });` — let Playwright retry.
options.explain: **Acceptable.** `toHaveCount` already retries by default, but extending the timeout is a valid stopgap. Better than `waitForTimeout` because it still fails fast on a real bug. Pair with the scroll fix for a robust solution.

stages.prompt: **Flaky test #3: `approve-expense.spec.ts`** — fails ~3% of the time, only on Mondays. Trace shows the test logged in as a manager, navigated to the approval queue, but the page rendered an empty state. The previous Friday's data should be there. Diagnosis?

options.label: It's test-data pollution between runs. The Friday seed run gets cleared by a Monday morning data-reset job. Fix: each test should create its own data via API and clean up after itself, never rely on shared seeds.
options.explain: **This is the right shape of fix.** Tests that depend on cross-run state are guaranteed to flake the moment something touches the shared state. Use Playwright's `test.beforeEach` with API setup so each test owns its data lifecycle.

options.label: Run the seed script before every test run as a CI pre-step.
options.explain: **Acceptable, weaker.** Re-seeding fixes the symptom but keeps the architectural smell (shared state across tests). Adds 30-60s to every CI run. Use only as a stopgap until you can refactor to per-test data.

options.label: Skip the test on Mondays.
options.explain: You discovered a real bug — the data-reset job is destroying state someone depends on. Skipping the test hides it. Tomorrow it'll be a customer who notices.

options.label: Disable the data-reset job.
options.explain: The job exists for a reason (probably compliance or storage cost). Disabling it 'because tests' is exactly how production systems get tangled. Fix the test, not the production housekeeping.

outcomes.perfect: All three flakes diagnosed correctly from trace files alone. Combined fix dropped CI red rate from 22% per PR to under 1.5%. Kavya posts in #engineering: *'Three flakes, three fixes, zero retries. This is the standard.'*
outcomes.good: You correctly diagnosed two of the three but reached for retries or sleeps once. Re-read the section on **trace-driven debugging** — the trace tells you the answer if you read it, every time.
outcomes.learn: You added retries or sleeps to mask the problem. The flake will return — usually right before a release. Re-read the lesson — especially **why retries are debt** and **how to read a Playwright trace step-by-step**.

points: Flake is information you haven't decoded yet. Treat it as a signal pointing at a non-determinism, not noise to suppress.
The trace viewer ritual: when a test flakes, open the trace before doing anything else. Set `trace: 'on-first-retry'` in your config.
The deterministic-clock fix: for tests that depend on time, install `page.clock` and advance virtual time. Real clocks make flaky tests.
Mock the network with `page.route()` instead of relying on real third-party services for tests that don't need them.
Retries are a temporary band-aid for genuine infra noise, not a substitute for fixing the actual cause.

blocks.md:
Every team that has ever shipped software has a story about *the suite that ate two engineers*: a Playwright project that started healthy in 2024, accumulated entropy through 2025, and by 2026 employed two full-time SDETs who did nothing but keep CI from going red. Their teammates called them maintenance heroes. The CFO called them a line item.

This is the lesson nobody teaches in tutorials. Writing tests is the easy part. Keeping a 312-test Playwright suite green for three years, across 14 release branches, while shipping features, *that* is the actual skill. It comes down to two named moves and the discipline to apply them every Monday.

blocks.title: Mental model: tests rot without a maintenance loop
blocks.md:
A test suite is not a deliverable; it's a **living artifact**. Every PR that lands changes the surface the tests cover. Every dependency upgrade changes the runtime. Every product pivot changes which flows are critical. Without an active maintenance loop, your suite gets slower, flakier, and less relevant *every single week*.

The right model: think of your suite the way an SRE thinks of a service. It has SLOs (flake rate, runtime, coverage of critical paths). It has on-call (someone owns triage when it goes red). It has a budget. It has a deprecation policy. If your suite has none of those, it's not a quality system — it's a graveyard with a CI pipeline.

steps.label: 1. CFO: 'Why are we paying 2 SDETs ₹24L/yr on test maintenance?'

blocks.md:
When CI takes 28 minutes, every team has the same dumb instinct: *delete some tests*. This is wrong. The right answer is **sharding**: split the suite across N parallel workers, run them in parallel CI jobs, and combine the results.

Playwright supports this natively. With 4 shards, your 28-minute serial run becomes a ~7-minute parallel run for the same coverage:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/test.yml
strategy:
  fail-fast: false
  matrix:
    shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
steps:
  - run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4
```

No tests deleted. No coverage lost. Same flake (now visible 4x faster, which makes it easier to fix). The only cost is CI minutes, which are usually cheaper than engineer time by an order of magnitude.

**The named move:** *sharding, not skipping.* When somebody says "the suite is too slow, let's delete tests" — push back with sharding first. Deletion is a last resort after measuring, demoting, and parallelising.

For configuration sanity, use the `projects` array in `playwright.config.ts` to split tests by browser or by tag:

```ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  fullyParallel: true,
  workers: process.env.CI ? 4 : '50%',
  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
    { name: 'mobile-safari', use: { ...devices['iPhone 14'] } },
    { name: 'critical', testMatch: /.*\.critical\.spec\.ts/ },
  ],
});
```

blocks.title: The classic trap: skipping tests to make CI green
blocks.md:
Every flaky test you `test.skip()` is a small lie you've told future-you. The skip survives the merge. The skip survives the next refactor. The skip is *still there in 2027* when someone else inherits the codebase and assumes it's intentional.

The rule: **skipping is allowed for one sprint, with an issue link in the skip comment.** If the issue is open after one sprint, the skip itself is a bug. Either the test was capturing real signal (un-skip and fix) or it wasn't (delete and document why in `DECISIONS.md`). The middle path — skip and forget — is how suites die.
