blocks.title: Field Notes: 88% Coverage, 14 Production Bugs, One Strategy Pivot
blocks.source: VP Engineering at Khaata Books, a Chennai-based small-business accounting SaaS (~₹120 Cr ARR, 3.2 lakh customers)
blocks.story:
Khaata's engineering org spent Q2 of 2024 chasing a board-mandated test-coverage target: **95% line coverage by year-end**. They started Q2 at 61% and finished at **88%**, on track to hit 95 by December. Engineers were measured on coverage delta in their PRs.

The problem: Q3 2024 shipped **14 critical-path bugs** to production. Wrong tax calculations on inter-state GST. Invoice PDFs missing the line-item totals on the second page. A reconciliation bug that hid ₹2.1 Cr of customer payments. None caught by the 88% coverage suite.

Why? Because the coverage was concentrated in the easy-to-test parts: utility functions, formatters, getters. The top-5 user journeys — invoice creation, payment recording, GST filing, bank reconciliation, year-end closing — had between **31% and 54% effective coverage** when measured by 'does a test exist that exercises this journey end-to-end with realistic data?'

In October the VPE killed the coverage target. Replaced it with: **'every top-10 user journey has at least one Playwright e2e spec, plus integration tests on every server action it touches, plus a golden-master test for any output the customer sees (PDF, CSV, email).'**

Q4 2024 shipped 6 critical bugs (down from 14). Q1 2025 shipped 4. Coverage % is now 79% and nobody cares — because the *right* 79%.
blocks.takeaway: Coverage measures what your tests touched, not what your customers care about. A 95% coverage suite that misses the top user journey is a 0% coverage suite where it counts.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The Coverage-vs-Impact Memo
blocks.setup:
Week 6, the final week. Sneha hit her targets: flake at 0.7%, CI at 11 minutes, suite cut from 289 specs to 84 well-chosen ones. The CTO **Vikram** is happy. The board is not.

The board read a McKinsey deck about 'engineering quality benchmarks' and now wants Tarakash to commit to **95% test coverage by end of FY26**. Vikram has scheduled a 30-minute meeting with Sneha to either align on the target or push back.

Sneha believes the 95% target is wrong. She has 24 hours to write a one-page memo arguing for an alternative. The memo will be read aloud at the next board meeting if Vikram is convinced.

coach.name: Staff-SDET Saurabh
coach.role: Has watched three companies hit their coverage targets and ship the same bugs anyway

stages.prompt: Sneha's memo opens with the **framing**. What's the strongest opening?

options.label: "95% coverage is achievable but it would not have prevented any of our last 8 production incidents. Here's what would have."
options.explain: **Strong.** You agreed the target is *achievable* (so the board doesn't think you're being defensive), then immediately pivoted to outcomes (which is what they actually care about). The 'here's what would have' creates anticipation — they have to keep reading.

options.label: "Coverage is a vanity metric. Real quality comes from culture, not numbers."
options.explain: Boards hate the word 'vanity' applied to their suggestions, and 'culture' has no measurement attached. You'll be dismissed as the engineering lead who 'won't be held accountable.' Lose the pitch in the first sentence.

options.label: "Per Google's testing blog and Kent Beck's recent essay, coverage targets above 80% have diminishing returns."
options.explain: Appeals to authority don't move boards. They have their own consultants who quote different authorities. Lead with *your* data on *their* business.

options.label: "To hit 95% coverage we need 4 more SDETs, ₹95 lakh of additional CI compute per year, and 6 months of work."
options.explain: You opened with cost without opening with the problem-with-the-goal. The board will counter-offer 'fine, hire two and we'll revisit' and now you've negotiated yourself into a worse outcome.

stages.prompt: The body of the memo needs **the alternative target**. What does Sneha propose?

options.label: "Every one of our top-10 user journeys has: (1) one Playwright e2e spec, (2) integration tests on every server action it touches, (3) a golden-master test on any customer-visible output. Currently 4 of 10 journeys meet this bar."
options.explain: **This is the answer.** Specific, measurable, customer-anchored, and honest about where you are today. The board can track 'journeys covered: 4 → 10' as easily as a percentage, but the metric actually maps to revenue.

options.label: "Replace coverage % with mutation-testing score above 80%."
options.explain: Mutation testing is technically excellent and the board will not understand a single sentence about it. They will ask three follow-up questions and walk away unconvinced. Use techniques the board can verify.

options.label: "Set the target at 70% coverage instead of 95% — same metric, lower bar."
options.explain: You accepted the framing (coverage % matters) and just argued for a worse number. The board will reasonably ask 'why not 80? Why not 90?' and now you're negotiating the wrong axis.

options.label: "Track production-incident rate (incidents per 1,000 deploys) with a target of <2."
options.explain: **Different angle, also valid.** Outcome metric ties tests to what the board actually wants (uptime, customer trust). Best used alongside the journey-coverage metric — one is leading, one is lagging.

stages.prompt: Vikram pushes back: *'The board likes round numbers. Can we just hit 95% and also do your journey thing?'* Sneha's response?

options.label: "We can — but the cost is ~28 weeks of engineering time we'd otherwise spend on the next 6 journeys. The marginal coverage will mostly be on code paths customers never see."
options.explain: **Lethal.** You quantified the opportunity cost in time the board understands (engineering weeks = features not shipped). You did not say 'no' — you said 'yes, but here's the trade.' Now Vikram has the words to take to the board.

options.label: "Sure, we'll do both."
options.explain: You just committed your team to two targets, one of which you don't believe in. In 6 months you'll either miss both or be remembered as the QA lead who burned out the team chasing a vanity number.

options.label: "No. The 95% target is wrong and I won't sign up for it."
options.explain: You're now the obstacle, not the solution. Vikram will champion someone who'll say yes, and you'll spend the next quarter being undermined.

options.label: "Let's pilot the journey metric for one quarter, report results to the board, and revisit the 95% target with that data."
options.explain: **Smart compromise.** A pilot defers the binary decision and lets evidence accumulate. The board feels heard ('we'll revisit'), you get a quarter to prove the journey metric, and the 95% target quietly dies if the pilot succeeds.

stages.prompt: Final paragraph — the **one-line summary** that gets read at the board meeting. Pick it.

options.label: "We propose tracking coverage of customer journeys, not lines of code, because customers experience journeys and don't experience lines."
options.explain: **Quotable.** A board member will repeat this in the next QBR. It frames the entire memo in one sentence and ties the technical decision to the customer outcome the board actually cares about.

options.label: "Test coverage is a complex topic that requires nuanced trade-offs."
options.explain: True, useless, and signals you're afraid to commit. The board will read this as 'engineering is making excuses.' Boards reward conviction, not hedging.

options.label: "Per industry research and our internal data, 95% coverage targets correlate weakly with quality outcomes."
options.explain: Accurate but boring. The board will skim past it and remember nothing. You need a line that lands, not a line that's defensible.

options.label: "The right question is not 'how much code did we test?' but 'did we test the code our customers depend on?'"
options.explain: **Reframes the entire debate.** Hard to argue with, easy to remember, ties to revenue. Either this or option (a) wins the board over.

outcomes.perfect: Vikram presents the memo to the board. They approve the journey-coverage pilot for Q1 FY26. By Q3, Tarakash's production incident rate is down 64% and the 95% coverage target has been quietly retired. Saurabh sends one Slack message: *'You changed how this company measures quality. That's a 6-week rescue that mattered.'*
outcomes.good: You made the right argument but pulled punches at one of the stages. Re-read the section on **opportunity-cost framing** — boards understand 'this costs you 28 weeks of features' better than any quality-philosophy argument.
outcomes.learn: You either accepted the 95% target or refused it without offering an alternative. In six months Tarakash will hit 95% coverage and ship the same incidents. Re-read the lesson — especially **why coverage % is a vanity metric** and **how to propose journey-based targets that boards can track**.

points: Tests rot without a maintenance loop. Treat your suite like a service: SLOs, on-call, budget, deprecation policy.
The failure-budget rule: a 1% flake rate target. When breached, feature work pauses until the top-5 are fixed.
Sharding, not skipping: parallelise CI before deleting tests. 4 shards turns a 28-min serial run into ~7 min for the same coverage.
`test.skip()` is allowed for one sprint with a tracked issue. Beyond that, the skip itself is a bug.
The Monday morning maintenance ritual — measure, identify, diagnose, decide, bound, document — keeps a suite alive for years.

assessment.title: Testing with Playwright Assessment
assessment.description: Tests your judgment across the test pyramid, Playwright selectors and waits, flake debugging, and CI discipline. Most questions have an 'almost right' option that mirrors the most common mistake; pick the one that survives a real codebase.

questions.stem: You're triaging a bug in production. Which is the *first* thing you write?

choices.label: The fix, then a test once verified
choices.explanation: Skips the proof you understood the bug. Half the time the fix solves a different problem and the original recurs.

choices.label: A failing test that reproduces the bug, then the fix
choices.explanation: The failing test is your evidence. The fix is then mechanical and the regression is locked out forever.

choices.label: A retry with `--retries=3` to confirm it's reproducible
choices.explanation: Retries hide bugs; they don't fix them.

choices.label: A Slack post asking who owns the code
choices.explanation: Sometimes useful, but not the first engineering action. Reproduce first.

questions.stem: A function calculates GST for a cart with 14 conditional branches across currency, payment method, and tax rules. What kind of test fits best?

choices.label: An e2e test that fills a real form and clicks Pay
choices.explanation: Wildly slow for what's essentially pure logic. The e2e proves wiring, not the 14 branches.

choices.label: A unit test with representative inputs for each branch
choices.explanation: Pure function, deterministic. Unit test runs in <5ms and covers the branching directly.

choices.label: An integration test against a real database
choices.explanation: GST calculation doesn't need DB. Integration adds cost without adding signal here.

choices.label: A snapshot test of the cart total UI
choices.explanation: Snapshot proves what the UI rendered, not whether the math is correct. Wrong altitude entirely.

questions.stem: Which Playwright locator is the right *first* choice for a 'Submit order' button?

choices.label: page.locator('.btn.btn-primary.submit-order-v2')
choices.explanation: Coupled to CSS classes; one design refactor and it dies.

choices.label: page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit order' })
choices.explanation: Role-based, name-based, framework-agnostic. The default.

choices.label: page.getByTestId('submit-order-btn')
choices.explanation: Test IDs are an escape hatch; reaching for them first skips the more semantic option.

choices.label: page.locator('xpath=//button[text()="Submit order"]')
choices.explanation: XPath in 2026 is a code smell. Almost always a better Playwright API exists.

questions.stem: A teammate pushes this code: `const t = await page.locator('h1').textContent(); expect(t).toBe('Welcome');`. What's wrong?

choices.label: Nothing — this is the standard pattern
choices.explanation: Not even close. The await breaks the auto-retry, making the assertion one-shot.

choices.label: The assertion no longer auto-retries; if the H1 renders 50ms later, the test fails
choices.explanation: Right. Use `await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toHaveText('Welcome')` instead.

choices.label: The H1 selector should be `page.locator('h1.title')` for specificity
choices.explanation: Adding more CSS coupling makes it worse, not better.

choices.label: The string 'Welcome' should be a regex
choices.explanation: Strings are fine. The retry break is the actual problem.

questions.stem: A test fails 3% of the time in CI. What's your first move?

choices.label: Add `await page.waitForTimeout(2000)` before the failing assertion
choices.explanation: Buries the signal under sleep. Next time the issue takes 2.1 seconds, you're flaky again.

choices.label: Open the trace viewer for the failing run and read the timeline + network panel
choices.explanation: The trace tells you in 60 seconds whether it's the test, the app, or your timing assumption.

choices.label: Bump `--retries` from 2 to 5 and ship
choices.explanation: Retries hide flake; they don't fix it. Slows CI for failing tests by 2.5x.

choices.label: Mark it `test.skip()` with a TODO comment
choices.explanation: The test had information for you. Now it's gagged.

questions.stem: Which signs suggest your suite is shaped like an ice-cream cone, not a pyramid? (Pick all that apply.)

choices.label: CI takes 28 minutes and most of it is a single e2e shard
choices.explanation: Top-heavy suite. Classic cone.

choices.label: You have more snapshot tests than logic tests for a pure data library
choices.explanation: Different bait, same culture: shape over substance.

choices.label: Devs run unit tests locally and let CI run e2e
choices.explanation: That's healthy. Fast tests local, slow tests in CI.

choices.label: Unit test failures cascade because of tight coupling between modules
choices.explanation: That's a coupling problem, not a pyramid problem.

questions.stem: You want to test a debounced search that fires after 300ms of inactivity. What's the right approach?

choices.label: `await page.waitForTimeout(500)` to be safely past 300ms
choices.explanation: Real time on CI varies by 200ms+. This is how 4% flake rates start.

choices.label: Install `page.clock` and advance virtual time with `clock.runFor(310)`
choices.explanation: Deterministic, fast, no CI jitter. The clock is yours.

choices.label: Bump `--retries` so the test eventually passes
choices.explanation: Retries paper over the timing race. They don't fix it.

choices.label: Use `expect(...).toBeVisible({ timeout: 30000 })` to give it lots of slack
choices.explanation: Slows the test, doesn't make it deterministic. The race condition is still there.

questions.stem: Which are *legitimate* reasons to use `--retries` in CI? (Pick all that apply.)

choices.label: Smoothing over a known-flaky CI runner so dashboards aren't all red while you fix it
choices.explanation: Acceptable as a temporary measure with a tracked deadline.

choices.label: As a final guard against transient blips with a third-party service you can't mock
choices.explanation: Acceptable when the third party is genuinely flaky and outside your control.

choices.label: To hide a debounce race so you can ship a PR before a demo
choices.explanation: Exactly the trap. Use `page.clock` and ship a real fix.

choices.label: Because the team agreed flakes are 'normal' and 3 retries usually works
choices.explanation: Cultural version of the trap. The day a real bug starts flaking 51% of the time, you ship it.

questions.stem: Your `playwright.config.ts` has `retries: 3` and `workers: 1` with 312 tests. CI takes 28 minutes. What's the highest-leverage single change?

choices.label: Drop retries to 0 to surface flake immediately
choices.explanation: Surfaces flake but turns CI red while you fix everything. Dev revolt within a week.

choices.label: Shard the suite across 4 workers/jobs in CI
choices.explanation: Sharding is the highest-leverage change: ~4x parallelism, no test changes, no surprises. Pair it with a failure budget.

choices.label: Delete the slowest 50 tests
choices.explanation: Loses real coverage. Demote them down the pyramid instead.

choices.label: Run only changed tests on each PR
choices.explanation: Brittle and incomplete; misses regressions in untouched code paths. Possible later, not first.

questions.stem: What does it mean to set a 'failure budget' for your test suite?

choices.label: A maximum number of tests allowed to fail in CI before the whole pipeline blocks
choices.explanation: Confuses budgets with thresholds. A budget governs *flake*, not pass/fail per run.

choices.label: An agreed maximum *flake rate* (e.g. 1%) above which the team stops feature work to fix tests
choices.explanation: Right. Budgets create a forcing function: when crossed, maintenance becomes priority over features.

choices.label: The maximum runtime the suite is allowed before being deleted
choices.explanation: Suites should be optimised, not deleted. Runtime budgets exist but aren't called 'failure budgets'.

choices.label: A monthly cost limit on CI minutes
choices.explanation: Useful but unrelated to test failure rates.

questions.stem: When should you reach for `page.route()` to mock a network request?

choices.label: Always — never hit real backends from Playwright
choices.explanation: Too absolute. E2E tests for the critical path *should* hit the real backend at least once.

choices.label: When the test depends on a third party that's slow, flaky, or charges per call
choices.explanation: Right: control the boundary, isolate the test, save the dollars.

choices.label: Only when the backend doesn't exist yet
choices.explanation: Too narrow. Mocks are valuable even when the backend exists.

choices.label: Never — mocks make tests lie about what the system does
choices.explanation: Real concern, wrong conclusion. Mock at the right altitude; keep one e2e for full integration.

questions.stem: Which of these are characteristics of well-written Playwright tests? (Pick all that apply.)

choices.label: Locators read like the user journey: 'click Pay, fill email, ...'
choices.explanation: Semantic locators describe behaviour, survive refactors.

choices.label: Most assertions are `await expect(locator).to...()` with no intermediate value extraction
choices.explanation: Web-first assertions retry; extracting first defeats the retry.

choices.label: Strategic `waitForTimeout` calls after each navigation 'just to be safe'
choices.explanation: Flake bombs. Auto-wait already handles navigation.

choices.label: All CSS selectors centralised in a `selectors.ts` file with comments
choices.explanation: Centralising bad selectors doesn't make them good.

questions.stem: Anita asks: 'we have 3 e2e tests for the same checkout flow with different inputs. Should I delete two of them?' What's the best answer?

choices.label: Yes, delete the redundant two
choices.explanation: Premature; you don't know yet which inputs catch real bugs vs which are duplicate.

choices.label: Demote the redundant inputs to a parametrised unit/integration test, keep ONE e2e for the critical path
choices.explanation: Right: same coverage at a lower altitude. Faster CI, less flake, no signal lost.

choices.label: Keep all three; e2e tests are precious
choices.explanation: All three at e2e altitude is exactly the cone-shaped suite problem.

choices.label: Add a fourth to cover edge cases
choices.explanation: Compounds the problem. More e2e is more flake surface.

questions.stem: A test passes alone but fails when run in parallel. The trace shows `getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })` matched 3 buttons. What's the root cause?

choices.label: Parallel runs aren't supported for this test
choices.explanation: Playwright supports parallel by default. The test isn't parallelism-incompatible; the locator is too broad.

choices.label: The locator is too broad; multiple dialogs each have a 'Save' button. Scope it to the relevant dialog.
choices.explanation: Right: `page.getByRole('dialog', { name: 'Edit profile' }).getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })`.

choices.label: Add `await page.waitForTimeout(1000)` so other tests finish first
choices.explanation: Anti-pattern: would make tests serial-by-sleep. Fix the locator scope.

choices.label: Mark it `test.serial` so it runs alone
choices.explanation: Hides the locator bug and slows CI by removing parallelism for no good reason.

questions.stem: You inherit a Playwright suite where coverage is 91% but a critical bug shipped to prod last week. Which of these are likely culprits? (Pick all that apply.)

choices.label: Most assertions use `toBeDefined()` or `toBeTruthy()` rather than specific behaviours
choices.explanation: These pass for almost any return value. Padding, not proof.

choices.label: The team chases a coverage number rather than asking what bug each test catches
choices.explanation: Goodhart: when the metric becomes the goal, you've lost the plot.

choices.label: The team uses Playwright instead of Cypress
choices.explanation: Tooling has nothing to do with this failure mode.

choices.label: There aren't enough e2e tests in the suite
choices.explanation: More e2e wouldn't have caught it; more *thoughtful* tests would have. Quality over altitude.

questions.stem: Your CTO asks: 'why does the suite take 28 minutes? Just delete the slow ones.' What's the best response?

choices.label: Yes, deleting the slowest 50 will get us under 15 minutes
choices.explanation: Loses real coverage. The slow tests usually exist for a reason; the fix is to demote, not delete.

choices.label: Sharding across 4 workers cuts wall time ~4x with zero coverage loss; deletion comes after triage, not before
choices.explanation: Right answer: parallelise first (free win), then triage what to demote down the pyramid.

choices.label: Tests don't matter; let's focus on shipping features
choices.explanation: Absolutely not. The CTO will quote that to the press during the next outage.

choices.label: Add `--retries=10` so we're more confident in the slow ones
choices.explanation: Compounds the slowness and the flake-hiding problem.

questions.stem: When refactoring an e2e test that uses `.locator('.btn-primary')`, what's the best replacement?

choices.label: `page.locator('button.btn-primary')` for more specificity
choices.explanation: Still coupled to CSS class; one rename and it dies.

choices.label: `page.getByRole('button', { name: <visible label> })`
choices.explanation: Role + accessible name. Survives style refactors.

choices.label: `page.getByTestId('btn-primary')`
choices.explanation: Test ID is the escape hatch; reach for role first.

choices.label: Wrap it in a helper function and call the helper everywhere
choices.explanation: Centralising bad selectors doesn't make them good.

project.title: Capstone: Rescue a 14% Flake Rate Suite in Two Sprints
project.prompt:
## The ask

You just joined a Pune-based B2B SaaS (let's call them **LedgerKite**, ~80 engineers, customers across Tier-2 India). The QA lead, Anita, drops a Slack on your second day:

> "Bhai, the e2e suite is on fire. **14% flake rate** over the last 30 days, **28-minute CI run** on every PR, devs are skipping it locally and force-merging on green retries. Two sprints. Fix it. The CTO is watching."

That's the entire brief. No code, no list of failing tests, no dashboard link. Anita is at a customer site for the next 48 hours.

## What you have

- 312 Playwright tests in TypeScript (mix of e2e, integration, and a few unit-shaped ones that snuck in)
- A `playwright.config.ts` with `retries: 3` and no sharding
- GitHub Actions running the full suite on every PR, 1 worker
- A `flaky-tests.csv` Anita exported: 41 tests with flake rates >5%
- The team has never used the trace viewer

## Deliverables (Markdown, ~800-1200 words total)

1. **Triage plan** — How do you classify the 41 flaky tests in week 1? What questions do you ask Anita when she's back? What do you measure before touching anything?
2. **The first 5 tests to rewrite** — Pick 5 representative failure modes (you can invent the test names; describe each in 2-3 sentences). For each, write the *fix pattern* in TypeScript Playwright (real APIs: `getByRole`, `waitForResponse`, `page.clock`, `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` etc.).
3. **The eval** — How will you know in 2 weeks whether you've actually improved things? Define 3 metrics with target numbers. Be honest about which one matters most.
4. **The rollback plan** — If your changes make things *worse* (slower, more flaky, devs revolt), what's the kill switch? When do you pull it?

## Constraints

- You cannot rewrite the whole suite. Pick your battles.
- You cannot add headcount. Anita and 2 SDETs are it.
- You cannot disable CI on `main`.
- Skipping a test counts as making the metric worse, not better.

The CTO will read this. Anita will defend it. Write like both are in the room.

levels.label: Triage logic is sound, fix patterns use real Playwright APIs correctly, metrics are measurable and tied to the actual problem
Mostly right but one fix pattern misuses an API or one metric isn't actually measurable
General shape is right but APIs are vague or metrics are vibes ('feels less flaky')
Recommends sleep statements, retries-as-fix, or 'just delete the flaky tests'
Reads like a senior SDET wrote it; named patterns, specific selectors, clear before/after, the rollback plan has a real trigger condition
Clear and structured but the rollback is hand-wavy or the fix patterns lack a named move
Functional but generic; could be about any tool, not specifically Playwright
Slack-message quality; bullet points without examples
Asks the right clarifying questions of Anita, accounts for the dev-revolt risk, names the failure mode where the fix itself becomes flaky
Handles 2 of 3 edge cases (missed clarifying questions OR no plan for dev pushback OR no second-order risk)
Treats the brief as fully specified; no clarifying questions, no rollback nuance
Ignores constraints (suggests adding headcount, skipping tests, or disabling CI)
